rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about an applicant's criminal record on an application, orally or in writing before making a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no time may providers evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records, or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer they may consider only the listed serious convictions and lifetime registration, plus indictable offenses within these lookbacks: 6 years for first degree, 4 years for second or third degree, and 1 year for fourth degree. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only on a preponderance-of-evidence finding that withdrawal serves a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must make an individualized assessment and give written reasons and an opportunity to appeal. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must give a written disclosure about criminal-history review. Providers may not require drug or alcohol tests. The act also bars discriminatory advertising and misuse of records. Enforcement is by complaint to the Division on Civil Rights only, not in court. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations, and return of the application fee may be ordered.
rules.key_value: Lookbacks 6/4/1 years by degree; records request within 30 days, provided free within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000/$5,000/$10,000; 14-day mediation window

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are enforced in summary proceedings in the Special Civil Part on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. The cap is adjusted each January 1 by CPI (NY-Northern NJ-Long Island, All Items), only if the change is greater than zero, and the Director publishes the limit. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee; penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent. Pet deposits and prepaid rent, including last month's rent, count toward the cap, so at most 2.5 months' rent may be required at lease inception. Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit stays the tenant's property in trust, is not commingled, and is held in an interest-bearing account at a New Jersey institution. Interest belongs to the tenant. Within 30 days of receipt, the landlord must give written notice of the bank, the amount, the account type and the rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% interest to rent. The deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions, must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends, by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. The deadline is 5 business days after displacement by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, and 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act termination. Tenants may recover double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees. A new owner is responsible for the deposit.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x monthly rent; increases max 10%/yr; return within 30 days; double damages

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A residential landlord may not evict, or fail to renew a lease, without one of the statutory good causes. These include:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- damage to the property
- breach of rules or lease covenants
- nonpayment of a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with local ordinances
- health and safety removal or illegal occupancy
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium or cooperative conversion, and owner or buyer occupancy after conversion
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking findings

A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment. Periods range from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause, and a Notice to Cease is required for some causes. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal may remove a tenant, and self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy receive relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent. Misuse of the unit after an owner-occupancy, retirement or demolition eviction brings treble damages, plus a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for residential reuse within 5 years. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same causes and notices under DCA regulations.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: 3 days to 3 years by cause; relocation assistance 6x monthly rent (illegal occupancy); treble damages; up to $10,000 civil penalty

coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel occupants with no alternate residence who live there continuously are covered. Rooming and boarding house owners must give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice (N.J.A.C. 5:26-3.4(c)).

rules.exemptions: Transient or seasonal hotel, motel or guest-house guests; units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member; owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings (narrower cause list only).
rules.effective_date_note: The guide states no effective date. The act (P.L.1974, c.49) is long-standing and in force.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit, and a longer lease must be honored until it expires. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with rental units must notify tenants in English and Spanish within 10 business days of the sale that ownership has changed and they need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. Cash-for-keys offers require a separate notice and a 5-day review period, and pressure tactics are prohibited.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit; tenant notice within 10 business days of sale; 5-day review period for buyout offers

coverage.summary: Applies to residential tenants of foreclosed properties, including month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only by foreclosure or the transfer of title after foreclosure.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide states no effective date.
rules.quoted_span: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey.
rules.review_note: For the 90-day notice to quit, the guide relies on case law (Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson) and cites no statute. The Foreclosure Fairness Act citation covers the notice and pressure-tactic duties.
rules.source_notes: Official DCA guide (D067), a secondary summary.

rules.title: Reprisal (anti-retaliation) protections for tenants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate by eviction, substantial alteration of the lease, or refusal to renew because a tenant exercised protected rights. Protected rights are: enforcing rights under the lease or law; making a good-faith complaint to a government authority after written notice to the landlord and a reasonable time to cure; organizing or joining a lawful tenant organization; and refusing lease changes made in retaliation. Tenants may sue for damages.

coverage.summary: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversion protections, including bar on conversion-cost rent increases)
rules.requirement: In a building converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, qualifying tenants may obtain protected tenancy and be protected from eviction for up to 40 years. Qualifying tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, or veterans with a 60% or higher service-connected disability. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the recording date and meet the income test. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of the right to apply, and applications are generally due within 60 days. Separately, for all tenants in a converted building, rents may not be raised to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed.
rules.key_value: Up to 40 years' protected tenancy; income not more than 3x the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; no rent increase to cover conversion costs

rules.exemptions: Rent increases for new services or amenities are not barred.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source-of-lawful-income protection in rental housing
rules.requirement: The Law Against Discrimination bars housing discrimination based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, along with other protected characteristics. A landlord cannot refuse a Section 8 voucher holder based solely on that source of income. Landlords may still refuse for insufficient income, an oversized family, a zoning-violating occupancy, or poor credit history. Complaints go to the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days at no cost, or to Superior Court within two years. Penalties reach $10,000 for a first offense.
rules.key_value: DCR complaint within 180 days or Superior Court within 2 years; penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense

coverage.other_conditions: The housing-for-older-persons and single-sex exceptions relate to familial status, not source of income.

rules.exemptions: Single apartment in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling; rooms in an owner- or occupant-occupied one-family home; religious-organization preference; housing for older persons (as to familial status only).

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
Under the New Jersey Antitrust Act, it becomes unlawful:
- for a rental property owner or its agent to pay for, subscribe to or contract for a coordinator's services
- for a coordinator to facilitate agreements restricting competition among rental property owners
- for anyone to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination
- for anyone to perform a coordinating function

A coordinating function means algorithmic or automated rent, lease-term or occupancy setting or recommending that uses competitors' nonpublic, competitively sensitive information, or common algorithms for two or more owners. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.key_value: Effective 2027-07-01; violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: A rental property owner is any person owning, directly or indirectly, one or more rental residential dwelling units.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units in NJ (houses, apartments, accessory units, other primary residences). Excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
coverage.other_conditions: Not a coordinating function: research or testing not used to set terms; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage databases that do not set or recommend rents; government affordability controls. Not an algorithmic device: non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data.

rules.exemptions: Research, statistical or testing uses; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases; government affordability controls; non-AI human-analysis spreadsheets; query-only databases.
rules.effective_date_note: First day of the twelfth month next following enactment (approved July 20, 2026), which is 2027-07-01. The act is not yet effective on the query date.
